new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record for Tai Phake has an empty rule and there are no existing statements. This work fills it: tone language (6 tones), no word-stress placement analysed; stress-related content limited to unstressed clitics/function words and unstressed non-final syllables of Pali loans. Identity caveat: the open copy is Morey 2005 (PL 565), the monograph from which the 2008 Routledge chapter was condensed; the 2008 chapter itself was not opened.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is given. The grammar treats Phake as a tone language with six lexical tones (Table 6.22, p. 127: 1 high level, 2 high falling, 3 low falling glottalised, 4 low falling, 5 low, 6 rising) and states on p. 113 that 'Tone is a crucial and obligatory feature of every Tai word.' It explicitly declines a prosodic (stress/intonation) analysis (p. 81). 'Stress' appears only as reduction: very common function words (reciprocal kan2, ka1 'go' as non-main verb, linker ko4, sün3 'if', nün1 'like', han2 'to') are 'usually unstressed' in connected speech with initial lenition and vowel reduction (pp. 117, 121); the proclitic pa1 in pa1 nan4 'there' / pa1 nai4 'here' is 'an unstressed form of the word paa1 'side'' (p. 209); and in polysyllabic Pali loans (sak1 ka1 rit1 'era', ta2 ti1 ya4 'third', a1 ni1 ca4 'changing') the non-final syllables are 'unstressed' and carry default level tone 1 while the final syllable carries tone 1, 2 or 4 (p. 133). My inference, not the author's statement: in polysyllabic loans the final syllable is the full-tone (prominent) one.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. The author raises but does not resolve 'whether there are toneless syllables in Tai Phake' (p. 133); notes that Khamti's revised alphabet has special marks for unstressed syllables (pp. 133, 196), which Phake does not.
new_statements.identity_note: The listed open copy (archive.org 'tai-languages-of-assam', 'The Tai Languages Of Assam (2005)') is Morey's 2005 Pacific Linguistics 565 monograph (CC BY-SA 4.0 online edition), not the 2008 Routledge chapter of the same title; the chapter was not obtained (DOI 10.4324/9780203641873 is a paywalled publisher record). The monograph's Phake data come from Namphakey (Namphake) village informants (Ee Nyan Khet, Aimya Khang Gohain, Yehom Buragohain), 1996-2000; Rose 1990 likewise records one female speaker from Namphake Gaon. Morey 2005 (LTBA) covers Phake alongside Aiton, Khamyang and Khamti; its stress remarks are about Aiton and Khamti.

tone_statements.quote: The present investigation found that the distribution of tones was the same as described by Banchob (1987) and Diller (1992), with some slight refinements regarding the exact quality of each tone. As with both Banchob and Diller, the principal informants for this study are from Namphakey village. Based on data collected in 1996-2000, the following tone chart (Table 6.22) is presented for Phake: ... 1 high level tone ma1 'shoulder'; 2 high falling tone ma2 'to come'; 3 low, falling tone, glottalised ma3 'mad'; 4 low falling tone ma4 'horse'; 5 low tone ca5 'for, to'; 6 rising tone ma6 'dog'

audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal; six lexical tones; no word-stress rule, 'unstressed' used only for function words in connected speech and medial syllables of Pali loans) rests on Morey 2005 PL-565, the standard reference grammar by the primary fieldworker, held as the publisher's open text; I re-opened it and every quoted fragment is verbatim at the stated sections/pages (pp.122, 127, 134). Glottolog's per-language list offers only Thai-university theses and a 9-pp conference phonology paper, none superior. Open instrumental/tonal literature downloaded now (Rose 1990 SST; Morey 2005 LTBA, scanned; Morey 2020 Himalayan Linguistics) uniformly describes a six-tone system with contrastive creak and says nothing about word stress, confirming the classification. No StressTyp2/WALS conflict exists. Nothing found suggests a reclassify; works still to obtain are low-priority confirmations only.

sources.quote: 'Tai Phake (Tai Kadai/Southwestern Tai) has six lexical tones, and nine phonemic vowels plus a length distinction between /a/ and /aː/ ... Tone 3 is creaky and is primarily distinguished from the others by phonation. Tone 4 is mid falling and short, whereas Tone 5 is mid falling and longer.' No occurrence of stress/accent/prominence anywhere in the paper (a full-text search for stress/accent).

tone.says: Per Morey 2005 sec. 6.2.4.3: about one hundred Phake words, nearly all tone-marked, with six tones described (Wilaiwan 1983: 231) as 1 low level then rising, 2 mid level, 3 mid falling glottalised, 4 high, 5 high level then falling, 6 mid; Morey derives a tentative tone box (Table 6.21) and judges the data 'not comprehensive enough' to be confident of it.

First-hand lexicographic tone notation.
